newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro court faults British military justice.
newsitem.headline: Euro court faults British military justice.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights faulted British military justice on Tuesday in the case of a Falklands war veteran who was dismissed from the army and jailed after holding fellow soldiers at gunpoint.
In a unanimous ruling by a nine-judge panel, the court concluded that the procedures used to try Briton Alex Findlay, 35, violated the European Convention on Human Rights.
The court said the British procedures were flawed because the court-martial board which tried him was insufficiently independent from the officer who conducted his prosecution.
Acting in anticipation of the verdict, Britain has revised its laws governing court-martial procedure, to take effect on April 1.

The rights court granted Findlay's request for reimbursement of nearly 24,000 pounds ($39,120) in legal fees but rejected his request for compensation for lost wages and suffering caused by his trial and the eight months he spent in prison.

"The court affirmed that it could not speculate as to what the outcome of the court-martial proceedings might have been had the violation of the convention not occurred. In consequence it did not award any compensation," it said in its judgment.

In July 1990, after a heavy bout of drinking while on duty in Northern Ireland, Findlay held members of his unit at gunpoint and threatened to kill them and himself. After firing two shots which injured no one, he surrendered and was arrested.
Psychiatric reports indicated that he had suffered post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from his experiences during the 1982 Falklands Islands war with Argentina.
A corporal in the Scots Guards, he witnessed horrific scenes in the fight for Mount Tumbledown, one of the fiercest battles of the short war on the disputed South Atlantic islands.
Findlay's lawyer argued that Britain had failed to develop treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder although it was recognised by many other countries.
In 1994, British authorities awarded Findlay 100,000 pounds ($156,000) in an out-of-court settlement as compensation for post-battle trauma.

Findlay had submitted his case to the Strasbourg-based European Commission of Human Rights in 1993, arguing that the 1991 court-martial sentencing him to jail and subsequent reviews of the case were unfair as those who sentenced him were neither independent nor impartial.
The commission, which screens cases for the court, concluded that Britain had violated Findlay's right to a fair trial, and passed his case on to the court.

The ruling is a new embarrassment for British justice, which suffered a heavy blow last week when three men jailed 18 years ago for the murder of a newspaper delivery boy were freed after prosecution lawyers agreed their trial had been flawed.

Britain has often been at odds with the European rights court. In 1995, the court condemned Britain for the killings of three unarmed Irish Republican Army guerrillas in Gibraltar in 1988. In 1996, it criticised Britain's rules for jailing minors.

In a separate ruling on Tuesday, the court cleared Britain of charges that it deprived a black man, David Gregory, of a fair trial in 1991 when he was sentenced to six years in jail despite his complaints that the jury was racist.
